query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Isothermal annealing of an as-cast MgAlCuZnGd lightweight HEA at moderate temperatures drives the nucleation and growth of Al-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries, which deplete Al from the matrix and alter local galvanic potentials and oxide-scale chemistry, thereby reducing both aqueous corrosion rates and high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium, supersaturated single-phase (B2/BCC) MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy, density <6 g/cm3
generation.intervention: Isothermal annealing at 400 °C for 1–100 h in inert atmosphere
generation.conditions: Exposure to 3.5 wt % NaCl solution at room temperature for corrosion testing and to 800 °C in air for oxidation testing
generation.structural_mediator: Volume fraction of Al-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Precipitation reduces the Al activity in the matrix and promotes formation of a more adherent, Al-enriched oxide scale while disrupting micro-galvanic coupling, leading to lower corrosion current and slower oxide growth
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will show ≥30 % reduction in corrosion current density and ≥25 % decrease in mass gain during 100 h oxidation at 800 °C compared to as-cast baseline
generation.baseline: As-cast, unannealed alloy tested under identical corrosion and oxidation protocols
generation.boundary: Valid for annealing between 300–500 °C and durations up to 100 h in alloys of similar composition and density <6 g/cm3
generation.uncertainty: Exact kinetics of precipitate formation and their precise composition are not fully quantified; effect sizes are approximate

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the MgAlCuZnGd HEA: one as-cast (baseline) and one annealed at 400 °C for 50 h. Characterize precipitate volume fraction by SEM/EDS and XRD, perform potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl, and conduct thermogravimetric oxidation at 800 °C for 100 h.
measurements: Precipitate volume fraction at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not show at least a 20 % increase in precipitate fraction or if corrosion current density and oxidation mass gain remain within ±10 % of the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
